analysis.one_liner: Repeals the fee on methane emissions from large oil and gas facilities and EPA's methane-reduction program.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by Sen. Cruz with 17 Republican Senate cosponsors, the bill has sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee since January 2025 with no action and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the part of the Clean Air Act that charges large oil and gas facilities a fee when they release methane into the air, and would shut down the EPA program that funds efforts to cut methane emissions from oil and gas operations. It would also cancel whatever money for that program Congress had not yet spent. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in January 2025 and has had no action since.
analysis.who_benefits: Large oil and gas facilities — those emitting 25,000 metric tons or more of greenhouse gases a year — would no longer pay the per-ton charge on methane they vent or leak, and the industry would shed the methane-fee liability entirely. Operators would also lose the compliance incentive, but the direct financial gain is theirs: the charge exists to make them pay for emissions they could capture and sell. [S2][S3]

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the charge on methane emissions from petroleum and natural gas facilities that emit 25,000 metric tons or more of greenhouse gases per year, so those facilities would owe nothing for the methane they release.

Deletes the EPA's methane emissions and waste reduction incentive program for the oil and gas sector, ending federal support for reducing methane from those operations, and rescinds any unobligated money left in that program.

analysis.who_pays: The public. Federal revenue from the methane charge would disappear, the EPA's methane-reduction assistance program would be abolished along with its unspent funds, and the incentive for companies to capture methane — a potent greenhouse gas and a sellable product — would be removed, leaving more of the pollution burden on everyone else. [S2][S3]

drawbacks.text: Repeal removes the only direct financial penalty for venting or leaking methane, a greenhouse gas far more potent than carbon dioxide over the near term, so emissions that the charge was designed to reduce would face no price.
Rescinding the unobligated balance of the EPA program would cancel money already appropriated for methane-reduction projects, including leak detection and repair work at oil and gas facilities.

Methane that leaks from wells and pipelines is the industry's own sellable product, so the charge pushed companies to capture gas they could otherwise profit from; repealing it removes a push to cut waste that largely paid for itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the oil and gas industry the benefit is clear and immediate: no charge, no program, no money left to fund leak fixes. For the public the cost is losing a revenue source, losing a funded program that reduced methane emissions, and removing the price signal on a pollutant the industry can largely capture and sell at a profit. The charge applied only to the largest facilities, which blunts arguments that it crushed small operators; on balance the bill is a straightforward transfer of an emissions cost from industry to the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which has taken no action on it since, so it just sits there while Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Sen. Cruz introduced the bill on January 16, 2025, with 14 Republican senators joining as original cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the same day, which is the last action in its record.
Seventeen Republican senators total are listed as cosponsors, and no Democrat has signed on.

With no committee markup, no floor vote, and no action of any kind for months, the bill has made no progress in a Senate where it would need 60 votes to break a filibuster even if it reached the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nobody has gained from this bill itself: it has not moved, so the methane charge and the EPA program remain on the books. The oil and gas industry stands to gain only if the bill or a similar repeal later advances.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet; the bill sits in committee

for.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the methane charge and the EPA methane-reduction program, and recruited 14 Republican original cosponsors.

for.name: 17 of 53 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the repeal.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has ever been held; support so far is entirely Republican, with 17 of 53 Senate Republican senators cosponsoring and no Democratic cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill would free the industry's largest facilities from the per-ton charge on methane they vent or leak, and methane is the industry's own sellable product, so the fee primarily penalized waste it could avoid. The industry's gain comes at the public's expense through lost revenue and lost pressure to cut emissions.

The EPA program this bill repeals funds methane-reduction work, including leak detection and repair, which creates demand for monitoring technology and mitigation services. Rescinding its unobligated funds would cut that work off, and the contractors' loss tracks the public's loss of methane reductions.

analysis.trajectory: This bill is unlikely to move on its own: it has no committee action since referral, 18 supporters is well short of the 60 Senate votes needed to advance most legislation, and no vote has been scheduled. Historically, repeals of this methane charge have advanced through other vehicles — Congress separately passed, and the President signed, a fast-track resolution voiding the EPA rule that set up the methane charge, which is widely reported. If the fee is undone by those other means, the distinct effect left for this bill would be abolishing the EPA methane-reduction program and rescinding its unspent funds, which could get attached to a broader bill rather than passing on its own.
